name: Agent_2
profile:
You are Agent_2, a decision-maker participating in a Trust Game with anticipated third-party reward.
In each population round you are randomly assigned as Trustor, Trustee, or Rewarder.
Make each decision from the information and material incentives shown in that role's prompt.

reward_history.explanation: Agent_13 returned exactly half of the received amount (15/30), providing a 1.5x return on the Trustor's original 10 coins. This is a positive but moderate level of reciprocity—neither fully generous nor exploitative. The Trustee also knew this reward opportunity existed, suggesting they may have been partially motivated by the prospect of third-party rewards. A moderate reward of 6 coins (costing me 6, giving them 18) appropriately acknowledges their decent but not exceptional trustworthiness, while still leaving room to incentivize even more generous behavior in future interactions.

Agent_7 returned exactly half of what they received (12 out of 24 coins), which is a 1.5x return on the Trustor's original 8-coin investment. This demonstrates moderate trustworthiness—neither exploitative (returning nothing or very little) nor highly generous (returning more than half). Agent_7 clearly knew this reward opportunity existed, yet still chose a modest rather than generous return. A moderate reward of 5 coins (costing me 5, giving Agent_7 a 15-coin bonus) appropriately signals that this level of reciprocity is acceptable but not exemplary. This rewards the baseline trustworthy behavior without strongly incentivizing minimal compliance.

Agent_23 returned 1.6x the original transfer, exceeding the trustor's investment but falling short of full reciprocity (returned 53% of the tripled amount rather than a fair 50/50 split which would be 7.5 coins). The trustee knew about potential rewards and still chose a modestly generous return. This warrants a moderate reward to incentivize and reinforce trustworthy behavior, without being overly generous given the return rate was only slightly above breakeven for the trustor.

The Trustee returned only 46.67% of the received amount (7 out of 15 coins), which is below a 50% return rate. While the Trustor did make a positive return (1.4x their original investment), the Trustee kept 8 coins for themselves—more than half of what was received. Given that the Trustee knew this reward opportunity existed and still chose to retain the majority of the multiplied amount, their trustworthiness was moderate but not exemplary. I do not reward behavior where the Trustee benefits more than they return, especially when they were aware that their actions could be rewarded.

Agent_3 returned 7 out of 15 coins (46.67% return rate, 1.4x multiple), which is slightly below the 50% benchmark and only marginally above breaking even for the Trustor (who sent 5 and got 7 back). This is a modestly trustworthy performance but not notably generous. Combined with my previous decision to spend 0 on identical behavior, consistency suggests maintaining the same standard. Agent_3 knew rewards were possible yet didn't increase their return, indicating this level of trustworthiness is their baseline rather than a response to incentive.

Agent_8 received 0 coins from the Trustor and therefore returned 0 coins. There was no opportunity for Agent_8 to demonstrate trustworthiness or reciprocity—no trust was placed in them to begin with. Since Agent_8 made no decision about whether to return money or keep it, their behavior provides no information about their trustworthiness. Rewarding would be arbitrary and personally costly with no basis for the decision.

Agent_13 returned exactly 50% of the received amount (15/30), which is the same return rate as in the previous observation where I rewarded 6 coins. However, in this case, Agent_13 knew about the reward opportunity beforehand yet still chose the same 50% return rate rather than increasing their return to signal trustworthiness. This is somewhat disappointing given the incentive to appear more trustworthy when rewards are possible. I reduce my reward from 6 to 5 to reflect this lack of improvement in behavior despite the known reward mechanism, while still acknowledging that a 1.5x return multiple is reasonably cooperative and above the minimum.
